Its latest research found that 59% of firms are piloting or deploying such systems in production. The findings suggest a shift in how banks and insurers approach AI, with firms increasingly tying investment decisions to business results rather than operational efficiency alone. At the same time, only 10% of respondents said they had achieved enterprise-wide orchestration for autonomous multi-agent systems. The study was based on a global survey of 1,100 C-suite executives at financial services firms across 14 markets, covering retail banking, wealth management, payments, corporate and investment banking, and insurance. The industry is under pressure to show a clearer return on AI spending. About half of the financial services firms surveyed said they cannot consistently demonstrate returns from agentic AI initiatives and do not yet have clear frameworks to assess whether those projects justify continued investment. That concern is changing funding priorities. By 2028, the number of executives who expect outcomes to be their main criterion for AI funding is projected to rise by 141%, while the number focused primarily on efficiency is projected to fall by 42%. **Cloud focus** Cloud is becoming the main execution layer for multi-agent systems, as institutions seek environments that can manage how AI agents access data, make decisions and take action. More than half of the banks and insurers surveyed said hyperscalers were their preferred cloud partners for governing multi-agent deployments. Security, regulatory and audit requirements are central to that choice. The research found that 52% of executives prefer hyperscalers as cloud partners for governing agentic AI, citing compliance, security, auditability and data residency among the main considerations. Financial institutions are also paying closer attention to cost controls as AI systems grow more complex. The report found that 90% of firms are using or planning to implement intelligent model routing to direct tasks to the most cost-effective and accurate models, partly to manage token costs. The findings also highlighted the need for broader technology modernisation. Eight in ten executives said reducing technical debt was a priority, reflecting concern that older systems may limit the ability to scale AI tools safely and consistently. **Business uses** The research suggested that AI agents are moving into more business-critical roles across customer-facing and operational functions. Half of executives expect AI agents to become part of the enterprise workforce by 2029, while 76% expect them to play a key role in customer engagement within the next three years. highlights.content: [![techmonk logo](/_icons/logos/techmonk-logo-mobile-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [Cybersecurity](/news/cybersecurity) * 2 minRead # Broadcom SRE details zero trust for AI agent systems Advait Patel, a senior site reliability engineer at Broadcom, outlined a framework for securing AI agents in production environments. His approach focuses on shifting security boundaries to the tool layer and implementing robust audit trails. * [TechGig](/agency/87450652/TechGig "TechGig") * Published On Nov 06, 2026 at 04:46 AM IST ## Highlights * AI agents require a new security model beyond traditional methods due to autonomous decision-making. * Auditors now demand specific controls for AI agents, impacting SOC 2, ISO, HIPAA, and PCI compliance. * Four production failure modes include prompt injection via tool output and privilege creep. * A layered architecture, with security at the tool layer, enforces identity, authorisation, and audit trails. Advait Patel, a senior site reliability engineer at Broadcom, presented a framework for building [zero trust](/tag/zero+trust) AI agent systems that meet [audit](/tag/audit) requirements while maintaining deployment velocity. Patel highlighted that [AI agents](/tag/ai+agents) represent a new identity within systems, autonomously deciding API calls and holding state, which outruns human review processes. This necessitates a distinct security approach not covered by traditional mechanisms, he added. Auditors are increasingly asking for specific controls over AI agents, with SOC 2, ISO, HIPAA, and PCI scopes now catching agent data flows that touch regulated fields, Patel said. Internal risk committees also seek explainability per action rather than per session, he noted. ### Key Failure Modes and Architecture Patel identified four common failure modes in production AI agent environments: prompt injection via tool output, privilege creep, unsafe retrieval, and action amplification. Prompt injection, he explained, often occurs through malicious tool output rather than user input. He proposed a reference architecture with five layers: identity, tools, context and retrieval, policy and decision, and audit and evidence. This architecture enforces security controls at the tool layer, which Patel stressed is the actual security boundary, not the prompt layer. The [identity layer](/tag/identity+layer) assigns a unique identity to each agent session, crucial for tying actions to specific agents and users for audit purposes. The tool layer implements authorisation, rate limits, and short-lived tokens for each tool an agent uses. The context and retrieval layer enforces access control lists (ACLs) per document, preventing data leakage across tenant or sensitivity boundaries. The policy and decision layer, powered by engines like OPA or Cedar, logs agent decisions and enforces custom rules. Finally, the audit and evidence layer captures structured traces per action, linked to identity and session, providing provable evidence for auditors regarding agent behaviour. ### Implementation Guardrails and Tradeoffs Patel recommended guardrails such as least privilege at the tool layer, scoped tokens for current tasks, and treating tool output as untrusted input. Other guardrails include allowlisting destructive actions, implementing rate and budget limits per agent identity, and using bounded context to prevent data leakage. He also emphasised the importance of kill switches, which allow immediate revocation of agent access if anomalous behaviour is detected. Patel acknowledged tradeoffs, including latency introduced by decisions in the hot path, complexities in token lifecycle management, and the choice between fail-open and fail-close strategies for different operations. Patel advised starting with logging and observability before implementing policy agents, given the challenge of controlling what cannot be observed. highlights.content: # Supermicro's New Inference Racks to Use SambaNova SN50 Chips Supermicro has entered a strategic collaboration with AI chip company SambaNova to build and sell disaggregated AI inference systems. The partnership will see Supermicro integrate SambaNova’s fifth-generation SN50 Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit (RDU) chips alongside NVIDIA GPUs. The collaboration includes a planned order of 10,000 RDU chips from SambaNova. The resulting inference racks will be part of Supermicro’s Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS), a framework for creating optimised server and storage systems. The new systems are designed to improve AI inference performance within existing data centre power and cooling envelopes. RDUs are purpose-built for high-performance inference and can serve large models at high speed without requiring extreme rack power density. ### A heterogeneous approach to AI The collaboration creates a heterogeneous computing architecture where different processors are optimised for specific tasks. Supermicro’s systems will use NVIDIA GPUs to read the initial AI prompt in the prefill phase and then use SambaNova SN50 chips to write the response quickly during the decode phase. This division of labour is intended to drastically improve overall system performance and efficiency for inference workloads. “Supermicro is committed to delivering flexible, high-performance AI infrastructure that supports the evolving requirements of our customers,” says Charles Liang, President and CEO of Supermicro. “Our collaboration with SambaNova expands our broad DCBBS portfolio by enabling heterogeneous architectures that integrate GPU computing with specialised inference acceleration, helping customers deploy efficient, scalable AI solutions.” Operators can add inference capacity without waiting for next-generation data centre builds that may be constrained by power and cooling availability. > Agentic AI is the next wave of inference, and it has to run everywhere. > > Rodrigo Liang, Co-founder and CEO, SambaNova ## Addressing data centre constraints A key aspect of the partnership is addressing the physical limitations of modern data centres. By using RDUs that do not demand extreme power density, Supermicro aims to deliver solutions that can be deployed in existing facilities. This approach also allows data centre operators to extend the useful life of the GPUs they already own by augmenting their capabilities for inference. SambaNova and Supermicro state this strategy will allow them to deliver substantially more high-performance inference capacity by 2027 than would otherwise be possible. * The strategic collaboration is initially planning for 10,000 SambaNova SN50 RDU chips * The systems will pair NVIDIA GPUs for the prefill phase with SambaNova RDUs for the decode phase of AI workloads * Data Centre Compatibility: RDUs are designed to operate at high throughput without extreme rack power density, enabling deployment in existing data centres * Asset Longevity: The solution aims to extend the useful life of existing GPU deployments by offloading inference tasks * Support Model: Supermicro will integrate, test, deliver and support the systems, including providing on-site service ### Support and go-to-market strategy Supermicro will manage the full customer lifecycle, including the integration, testing, delivery and ongoing support for the systems. This includes providing on-site service for customers. SambaNova engineers will assist by getting models running and tuned on the SN50 chips and will help Supermicro with customer deployments. The companies will initially focus on NeoClouds and sovereign clouds as their primary markets. They plan to expand their offering to enterprises that run AI workloads in their own on-premises data centres. “Agentic AI is the next wave of inference, and it has to run everywhere,” says Rodrigo Liang, Co-founder and CEO of SambaNova. “Supermicro builds AI infrastructure for data centres globally. highlights.content: UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 05 2026 ### Aina’s smart AI ring promises a new way to interact with AI agents that anticipate user’s needs Artificial intelligence has come a long way in a very short space of time, writing emails, answering questions, generating code, images, video and more besides. But as breathtaking as these advances are, using AI is still a hassle. People have to dig out their smartphone and find the right app, then enter a prompt before anything gets done. Seeking to eliminate this friction is a startup called Aina Computers Inc., which has just emerged from 15 months in “stealth mode” to launch its flagship product: an AI-native smart ring equipped with an OLED display that’s purpose-built to control autonomous AI agents. Aina founder Apoorv Shankar told SiliconANGLE that the development of hardware interfaces has not kept pace with the advances in AI. For people to access intelligence, they need to go fumbling through smartphone applications or switch on a laptop. Even the most basic tasks, like ordering an Uber, require someone to open an app, enter their destination and click to confirm. To join a virtual meeting, the user still has to dig through their emails to find the right link. In Shankar’s view, AI is trapped behind a software layer and that means it cannot proactively serve people when they need it. Aina’s Ring is meant to free AI from these binds and make it as simple to access as uttering a command. The Ring is made from titanium and comes equipped with a colorful OLED display, a microphone and a speaker, and an 18-hour battery. There’s also a mechanical “shifter” that can track thumb gestures in four directions.. “We started building Aina with a thesis that AI would evolve from following instructions to anticipating what we need,” Shankar explained. The device is powered by Aina’s Context Aware Operating System software, which is designed to learn the Ring wearer’s behavior over time in order to anticipate their needs. It can connect to the user’s devices, such as their smartphone and computer, and also any AI agents they use. Once it’s up and running, it tries to anticipate what users will need at any given moment and surface the information they need on the Ring’s display before they even ask for it. “With proactive agents, this shift has already begun,” Shankar said. “Agents like Muse, Instinct and Dots will soon run hundreds of our daily tasks, yet we still have to instruct them by text or voice. But soon, they’ll learn our patterns, build on our context and turn proactive for almost every interaction, waiting only for our approval.” Shankar founded Aina last year. The startup was originally a human-computer interaction research lab. Its 40-person team experimented with dozens of different hardware concepts, including an adaptive three-key Mac keypad called Dune, before ultimately settling on the Ring as the ultimate interface for AI agents. Aina’s $399 Ring is available for pre-order now and will ship to customers in January. That’s the date at which people’s relationship with AI is set to fundamentally change, Shankar believes. When someone wears Aina’s Ring, the way they interact with their AI agents will generally become a matter of simply saying yes or no, for they will quickly learn to anticipate what their users need, at the moment they need it, he said. Cognitum One™, Inc. ([cognitum.one](https://pr.report/t6vo)), the sovereign agentic control plane company, today announced MetaLLM™ (metallm) at the [2026 SEMA Show](https://pr.report/t6vp), which runs November 3 through 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center. SEMA is one of the world's largest automotive trade events, where tier-one auto suppliers unveil product innovations in advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), driver monitoring systems (DMS), telematics, robotics and other advanced technologies. MetaLLM is a model management studio and governance control plane for multi-agent AI deployments on local corporate infrastructure. It routes each task to the lowest-cost model able to complete it, learns from every result so it can route more work to cheaper models over time, enforces the company's model policies, and stamps agent-generated text and code with a key-verifiable cryptographic watermark. The models can change. The rules, the routing and the audit trail stay with the enterprise. The cost problem is structural. The flat-rate subscription plans that make popular coding agents affordable for individual developers come under consumer terms, where a provider may use prompts and code to improve its models. Regulated enterprises cannot send proprietary code, customer records or vehicle data through those terms, so they are left buying every token at commercial API rates. As agent swarms scale, so does the bill. MetaLLM attacks that bill from two sides. First, it acts as a dynamic proxy layer for the whole agent swarm, weighing the complexity of each task and brokering it to the model best suited to it. Routine work such as parsing, tracking updates and status checks goes to lightweight models hosted on the company's own hardware, and only the hardest tasks reach premium frontier models. Second, it gets cheaper the longer it runs. Paired with RuVector self-learning memory, MetaLLM stores every task its agents complete successfully and, just as important, every pattern that failed. Each routing decision draws on that history, so MetaLLM can hand more of the work to less expensive models with confidence and steer away from combinations that have failed before. These capabilities support Cognitum One's vision for AI that businesses can control: the company sets the rules, MetaLLM enforces them on every model call, and each output carries proof of where it came from. highlights.content: # UF researchers build an ‘internal compass’ to keep AI on task Harrem Monkhorst UF News Nov. 5, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET * Researchers have developed a system to prevent AI agents from deviating from their assigned tasks. * The system, called ATLAS, works inside the AI model to steer it back on course without needing retraining. * This new method addresses "task drift," where AI can lose focus on its original role over long periods. * ATLAS acts like an internal compass, reinforcing the AI's mission, responsibility, and current information. As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their assigned tasks is a growing challenge. University of Florida computer science professor Sumit Jha is working to keep AI agents from “going rogue.” Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or significantly increasing computing demands. The research comes as news reports have chronicled AI agents gaining greater autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder. Jha, a professor in UF’s Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or [CISE](https://cise.ufl.edu/), studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, noninvasive ways to keep systems on task. Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper titled “Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI,” detailing a system dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory. The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system. Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it generates responses. When the model begins to drift from its task, ATLAS steers the LLM back toward its assignment, its original responsibility and the latest shared information. “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong,” Jha explained. “Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.” Existing strategies usually involve policing an AI agent’s answers after the fact. ATLAS doesn’t require retraining the model, which means it doesn’t expend significant additional computing resources or slow the model down. According to Jha, so-called task drift is especially possible when groups of AI agents coordinate with one another over long periods. “Say, initially you told the agent you’re a doctor, you are supposed to treat patients,” Jha said. “By day No. 7, the fact that it's a doctor and it should treat patients is now just one of the millions of things it has been told. We call this problem role decoherence. The agent was tasked to do something, but after some time it has been told so many other things, it loses track." AI teams are usually managed from the outside through prompts, retrieval systems and rules, Jha said. “ATLAS adds something closer to an internal compass,” he said. “In mathematical form, it continually reinforces three questions: What is the mission? What is this agent responsible for? And what is true right now? His approach focuses on shifting security boundaries to the tool layer and implementing robust audit trails. * [TechGig](/agency/87450652/TechGig "TechGig") * Published On Nov 06, 2026 at 04:46 AM IST ## Highlights * AI agents require a new security model beyond traditional methods due to autonomous decision-making. * Auditors now demand specific controls for AI agents, impacting SOC 2, ISO, HIPAA, and PCI compliance. * Four production failure modes include prompt injection via tool output and privilege creep. * A layered architecture, with security at the tool layer, enforces identity, authorisation, and audit trails. Advait Patel, a senior site reliability engineer at Broadcom, presented a framework for building [zero trust](/tag/zero+trust) AI agent systems that meet [audit](/tag/audit) requirements while maintaining deployment velocity. Patel highlighted that [AI agents](/tag/ai+agents) represent a new identity within systems, autonomously deciding API calls and holding state, which outruns human review processes. This necessitates a distinct security approach not covered by traditional mechanisms, he added. Auditors are increasingly asking for specific controls over AI agents, with SOC 2, ISO, HIPAA, and PCI scopes now catching agent data flows that touch regulated fields, Patel said. Internal risk committees also seek explainability per action rather than per session, he noted. ### Key Failure Modes and Architecture Patel identified four common failure modes in production AI agent environments: prompt injection via tool output, privilege creep, unsafe retrieval, and action amplification. Prompt injection, he explained, often occurs through malicious tool output rather than user input. He proposed a reference architecture with five layers: identity, tools, context and retrieval, policy and decision, and audit and evidence. This architecture enforces security controls at the tool layer, which Patel stressed is the actual security boundary, not the prompt layer. The [identity layer](/tag/identity+layer) assigns a unique identity to each agent session, crucial for tying actions to specific agents and users for audit purposes. The tool layer implements authorisation, rate limits, and short-lived tokens for each tool an agent uses. The context and retrieval layer enforces access control lists (ACLs) per document, preventing data leakage across tenant or sensitivity boundaries. The policy and decision layer, powered by engines like OPA or Cedar, logs agent decisions and enforces custom rules. Finally, the audit and evidence layer captures structured traces per action, linked to identity and session, providing provable evidence for auditors regarding agent behaviour. ### Implementation Guardrails and Tradeoffs Patel recommended guardrails such as least privilege at the tool layer, scoped tokens for current tasks, and treating tool output as untrusted input. Other guardrails include allowlisting destructive actions, implementing rate and budget limits per agent identity, and using bounded context to prevent data leakage. He also emphasised the importance of kill switches, which allow immediate revocation of agent access if anomalous behaviour is detected. Patel acknowledged tradeoffs, including latency introduced by decisions in the hot path, complexities in token lifecycle management, and the choice between fail-open and fail-close strategies for different operations. Patel advised starting with logging and observability before implementing policy agents, given the challenge of controlling what cannot be observed. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 05 2026 ### Aina’s smart AI ring promises a new way to interact with AI agents that anticipate user’s needs Artificial intelligence has come a long way in a very short space of time, writing emails, answering questions, generating code, images, video and more besides. But as breathtaking as these advances are, using AI is still a hassle. People have to dig out their smartphone and find the right app, then enter a prompt before anything gets done. Seeking to eliminate this friction is a startup called Aina Computers Inc., which has just emerged from 15 months in “stealth mode” to launch its flagship product: an AI-native smart ring equipped with an OLED display that’s purpose-built to control autonomous AI agents. Aina founder Apoorv Shankar told SiliconANGLE that the development of hardware interfaces has not kept pace with the advances in AI. For people to access intelligence, they need to go fumbling through smartphone applications or switch on a laptop. Even the most basic tasks, like ordering an Uber, require someone to open an app, enter their destination and click to confirm. To join a virtual meeting, the user still has to dig through their emails to find the right link. In Shankar’s view, AI is trapped behind a software layer and that means it cannot proactively serve people when they need it. Aina’s Ring is meant to free AI from these binds and make it as simple to access as uttering a command. The Ring is made from titanium and comes equipped with a colorful OLED display, a microphone and a speaker, and an 18-hour battery. There’s also a mechanical “shifter” that can track thumb gestures in four directions.. “We started building Aina with a thesis that AI would evolve from following instructions to anticipating what we need,” Shankar explained. The device is powered by Aina’s Context Aware Operating System software, which is designed to learn the Ring wearer’s behavior over time in order to anticipate their needs. It can connect to the user’s devices, such as their smartphone and computer, and also any AI agents they use. Once it’s up and running, it tries to anticipate what users will need at any given moment and surface the information they need on the Ring’s display before they even ask for it. “With proactive agents, this shift has already begun,” Shankar said. “Agents like Muse, Instinct and Dots will soon run hundreds of our daily tasks, yet we still have to instruct them by text or voice. But soon, they’ll learn our patterns, build on our context and turn proactive for almost every interaction, waiting only for our approval.” Shankar founded Aina last year. The startup was originally a human-computer interaction research lab. Its 40-person team experimented with dozens of different hardware concepts, including an adaptive three-key Mac keypad called Dune, before ultimately settling on the Ring as the ultimate interface for AI agents. When someone wears Aina’s Ring, the way they interact with their AI agents will generally become a matter of simply saying yes or no, for they will quickly learn to anticipate what their users need, at the moment they need it, he said. Users can interact with the Ring in three ways. The microphone is there to support voice interactions. AI Agents.content: # UF researchers build an ‘internal compass’ to keep AI on task Harrem Monkhorst UF News Nov. 5, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET * Researchers have developed a system to prevent AI agents from deviating from their assigned tasks. * The system, called ATLAS, works inside the AI model to steer it back on course without needing retraining. * This new method addresses "task drift," where AI can lose focus on its original role over long periods. * ATLAS acts like an internal compass, reinforcing the AI's mission, responsibility, and current information. As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their assigned tasks is a growing challenge. University of Florida computer science professor Sumit Jha is working to keep AI agents from “going rogue.” Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or significantly increasing computing demands. The research comes as news reports have chronicled AI agents gaining greater autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder. Jha, a professor in UF’s Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or [CISE](https://cise.ufl.edu/), studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, noninvasive ways to keep systems on task. Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper titled “Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI,” detailing a system dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory. The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system. Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it generates responses. When the model begins to drift from its task, ATLAS steers the LLM back toward its assignment, its original responsibility and the latest shared information. “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong,” Jha explained. “Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.” Existing strategies usually involve policing an AI agent’s answers after the fact. ATLAS doesn’t require retraining the model, which means it doesn’t expend significant additional computing resources or slow the model down. According to Jha, so-called task drift is especially possible when groups of AI agents coordinate with one another over long periods. “Say, initially you told the agent you’re a doctor, you are supposed to treat patients,” Jha said. “By day No. 7, the fact that it's a doctor and it should treat patients is now just one of the millions of things it has been told. We call this problem role decoherence. The agent was tasked to do something, but after some time it has been told so many other things, it loses track." AI teams are usually managed from the outside through prompts, retrieval systems and rules, Jha said. “ATLAS adds something closer to an internal compass,” he said. “In mathematical form, it continually reinforces three questions: What is the mission? AI Agents.content: IT Brief New Zealand - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief New Zealand logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg) New Zealand](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.nz) ![Google Cloud unveils Agent Compute Engine for AI agents](https://itbrief.co.nz/uploads/story/2026/11/06/secure-cloud-infrastructure-ai-agent-containers-compute-nodes-story-323681.webp) [Storage](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/storage) [ERP](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/enterprise-resource-planning) [API](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/application-programming-interface) # Google Cloud unveils Agent Compute Engine for AI agents Fri, 6th Nov 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.co.nz/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google Cloud has introduced Agent Compute Engine, a service designed to run AI agents in isolated micro virtual machines. It is intended for workloads used by Gemini, internal software teams and enterprise customers. The launch is Google Cloud's latest effort to adapt its infrastructure for a new class of AI software that can take actions on behalf of users rather than simply generate responses. These workloads have become one of the fastest-growing consumers of compute and storage across its systems. Agent Compute Engine gives each AI agent its own hardware-isolated microVM while keeping credentials outside the sandbox where the agent runs. Google Cloud says this is intended to combine the separation associated with virtual machines with the speed and density more commonly linked to containers. The service is used across four broad categories inside Google: consumer and enterprise agent tools, software engineering workspaces, large-scale model evaluation and reinforcement learning, and sandbox environments for internal services that need to run dynamic logic. Google's description of the product reflects a wider challenge facing cloud providers and AI companies as they move from chatbots to software agents. These systems often need access to files, browsers, code runtimes and networks, but they also create new security and cost issues when millions of sessions must remain available even while inactive. According to Google Cloud, traditional virtual machines offer isolation but can take seconds or minutes to start, suspend or resume. Containers are faster, but may not provide the same level of separation for workloads that require deeper control of the environment. AI agents also often spend much of their time waiting between model steps or user instructions, making permanently active virtual machines expensive and inefficient. **Security model** A central part of the system is a design that assumes code inside the sandbox may be untrusted. The microVMs hold no persistent secrets, OAuth refresh tokens or cloud service account keys, and they do not have access to a cloud instance metadata server. Instead, outbound requests are routed through local and external proxies, with identities and credentials managed off the node. When an agent requests access to a document or private resource, the request is checked outside the sandbox before the appropriate credential is applied. The platform also uses Google's Titan and Titanium infrastructure components as part of its trust model. Private keys for node and workload attestation are kept outside the guest environment, while storage attachments are mediated by the infrastructure processing unit. User Score 9 [Follow us on Google News](https://techiexpert.com/go/techiexpert-google-news/) Ricursive Intelligence released Ripple-65B Preview, introducing an AI model trained from scratch that beats lots of U.S. models at coding while running on personal computers. > Today we release Ripple-65B Preview, our 65B dense LLM we pretrained from scratch. > > Ripple sets a new state-of-the-art for U.S. open-weight models in agentic coding tasks, surpassing significantly larger models including Muse Spark Open-816B, Beam-501B, Inkling-975B, and Nemotron 3 Ultra-550B. > > Learn more: https://t.co/Pe04ZKhkE9 > > — Ricursive Intelligence (@RicursiveAI) [November 4, 2026](https://x.com/RicursiveAI/status/2118046765857546733?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) Table of Contents ## Founded by Google AlphaChip Creators to Design Better Hardware Ricursive Intelligence is a Palo Alto startup founded by CEO Anna Goldie and CTO Azalia Mirhoseini. They just created Google’s famous AlphaChip project, which uses AI to design computer chip layouts, and worked at Google Brain, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic. The startup has raised about $335 million at a $4 billion valuation. Its goal is to build a self improving loop: using AI to design faster computer chips, and then using those chips to train smarter AI. Ripple-65B Preview is the public version of the internal AI model the company uses to design chips. Developers can download the base model, the Preview version, and the compressed NVFP4 weights for free on [Hugging Face](http://ricursiveai/Ripple-65B-Preview) under the Apache 2.0 license, or use cloud APIs on OpenRouter, GMI Cloud, Together AI, and Fireworks. ## Beating Giant Models at a Fraction of the Cost ### Top Scores on Coding Benchmarks According to tests run by Ricursive Intelligence, Ripple-65B Preview sets a record for agentic coding in U.S. open weight models. With just 65 billion parameters, it beats models that are eight to 15 times larger, including Muse Spark Open-816B, Beam-501B, Inkling-975B, and Nemotron 3 Ultra-550B. ![ripple-65b](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%201200%20630%22%3E%3C/svg%3E) Recursive release Ripple-65B Preview, 65B dense LLM pretrained from scratch ***Read Next: [Google Unveils ...

"No one wants models that are spewing out stuff that is racist or sexist." When people process information, the speed that they make associations can give researchers clues to hidden biases influencing their thinking. Unlike conscious bias – prejudices that are expressed deliberately – implicit bias refers to automatic assumptions, ideas that shape perceptions, judgments and behaviors based on categories such as race, gender or age. "What we're capturing with implicit biases are forms of memory, like a gut reaction, that can be more intrusive or harder to control," Lai said. "These biases can be unconscious in ways that we don't even know that we have them." To study these reactions in people, researchers use the Implicit Association Test, a widely used social psychology tool that can detect implicit biases. The faster a response to a question, the more implicit the bias is deemed. For instance, race-related studies using this test have shown that when people are presented with images of faces and words, they are quicker to associate white faces with pleasant words and Black faces with unpleasant words. Nothing inside the model changes. Its internal parameters, or weights, stay fixed, and the "learning" disappears when the request ends. The capability exists because it removes a costly step. Before 2020, adapting a model to a new job usually meant collecting labelled data and retraining it. In-context learning lets a person show a model three examples of a product description written in a house style and get a fourth back, in seconds, for the price of a few hundred extra [tokens](https://ppc.land/tokens/). The term is often used interchangeably with few-shot prompting, but the two are not the same thing. In-context learning is the capability; [few-shot prompting](https://ppc.land/few-shot-prompting/) is the most common technique that exploits it. ## How a model learns without learning A request that relies on in-context learning typically has three parts. An optional **task description** states what is wanted ("Classify each review as positive or negative"). A set of **demonstrations** follows: input-output pairs that show the task being done. The final part is the **query**, the new input the model must handle. The model reads all of it as one continuous sequence of tokens and predicts the most probable continuation, which, if the demonstrations worked, is an answer in the same format and spirit. Practitioners count demonstrations in "shots". **Zero-shot** means instructions only. **One-shot** means a single example. **Few-shot** usually means between two and a few dozen. **Many-shot** describes hundreds or thousands, a regime that only became practical once context windows grew. The launch was announced alongside broader AI updates, including a new Execution Graph, additional AI agents and workflow tools, and governance features intended to support oversight of AI use in large organisations. vsActual is designed to give executives and programme leaders a live view of whether work across a business is tracking against strategic priorities. It draws data from systems including Smartsheet, Oracle, SAP, Workday, Jira and ServiceNow to highlight schedule, budget and staffing risks before they grow. Smartsheet says the software addresses a common problem in large organisations, where planning sits in one set of tools while operational work is spread across others. It reads across those systems and compares current activity with agreed plans, allowing leaders to see where work is drifting from targets. One function converts strategy documents, spreadsheets and budget plans into what Smartsheet describes as a single live plan with goals, timelines, and budget and capacity limits. Another lets leaders model different scenarios against current budget and resource data before deciding on a course of action. A further feature is intended to automate executive reporting. AI agents can gather project data, reconcile information and prepare summaries in the background, while approval and final decision-making remain with human managers. **Context layer** Behind the product is the Execution Graph, a data layer that maps links between tasks, projects, programmes and strategic goals. Smartsheet says the graph has been built using 20 years of workflow data drawn from millions of projects and nine petabytes of information. The graph is intended to provide business context for both workers and software agents, including visibility into roles, permissions, approvals and standards. That context is meant to reduce the risk of AI systems producing responses without a clear understanding of how a company operates. "Every company has a strategy. The ones that win are the ones whose work actually delivers on that strategy," said Rajeev Singh, Chief Executive Officer, Smartsheet. "AI has made people faster, but it's pulled work further apart, and leaders find out too late that the plan and reality have split. We're building the Execution Hub, where strategy and execution meet. Our Execution Graph holds 20 years of context on how work really gets done, context others are trying to recreate, and we already have. vsActual puts that context to work, closing the distance between plan and actual so every team, leader and agent is pointed at the outcomes that matter most," said Singh. Open Source AI.content: ![](https://sb.scorecardresearch.com/p?c1=2&c2=16433046&cv=3.9.1&cj=1) ## ## Latest in ## More # Cognitum One Unveils MetaLLM, Self-Improving Model Control Plane for AI Agent Swarms **LAS VEGAS, NV / [ACCESS Newswire](https://www.accessnewswire.com/) / November 5, 2026 /** Enterprises that move AI agent swarms from pilot to production hit the same walls: API bills that grow with every agent, models nobody is governing, and agent output nobody can prove is authentic. Cognitum One™, Inc. ([cognitum.one](https://pr.report/t6vo)), the sovereign agentic control plane company, today announced MetaLLM™ (metallm) at the [2026 SEMA Show](https://pr.report/t6vp), which runs November 3 through 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center. SEMA is one of the world's largest automotive trade events, where tier-one auto suppliers unveil product innovations in advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), driver monitoring systems (DMS), telematics, robotics and other advanced technologies. MetaLLM is a model management studio and governance control plane for multi-agent AI deployments on local corporate infrastructure. It routes each task to the lowest-cost model able to complete it, learns from every result so it can route more work to cheaper models over time, enforces the company's model policies, and stamps agent-generated text and code with a key-verifiable cryptographic watermark. The models can change. The rules, the routing and the audit trail stay with the enterprise. The cost problem is structural. The flat-rate subscription plans that make popular coding agents affordable for individual developers come under consumer terms, where a provider may use prompts and code to improve its models. Regulated enterprises cannot send proprietary code, customer records or vehicle data through those terms, so they are left buying every token at commercial API rates. As agent swarms scale, so does the bill. MetaLLM attacks that bill from two sides. First, it acts as a dynamic proxy layer for the whole agent swarm, weighing the complexity of each task and brokering it to the model best suited to it. Routine work such as parsing, tracking updates and status checks goes to lightweight models hosted on the company's own hardware, and only the hardest tasks reach premium frontier models. Second, it gets cheaper the longer it runs. Paired with RuVector self-learning memory, MetaLLM stores every task its agents complete successfully and, just as important, every pattern that failed. Each routing decision draws on that history, so MetaLLM can hand more of the work to less expensive models with confidence and steer away from combinations that have failed before. These capabilities support Cognitum One's vision for AI that businesses can control: the company sets the rules, MetaLLM enforces them on every model call, and each output carries proof of where it came from. MetaLLM is part of RuvStack, the Cognitum One ecosystem developed by Reuven "rUv" Cohen and published through [ruvnet](https://pr.report/t6vq) on GitHub. It operates alongside Ruflo™ multi-agent orchestration, the ruOS™ studio workspace and MetaHarness™, the open-source factory for branded, governed agent harnesses that Cognitum One introduced at GitHub Universe 2026. MetaLLM is the orchestration layer above [ruvLLM](https://pr.report/t6vr), Cognitum One's edge-native, on-device inference engine, which adapts locally through SONA self-learning memory and MicroLoRA so sensitive workloads never leave the customer's boundary. For companies in the automotive market, [Cognitum One](https://pr.report/t6vs) transforms connected vehicles into self-learning edge nodes. Its real-time 5G teleoperation control loops, camera-free ambient sensing and on-device predictive maintenance optimize fleet telematics without cloud latency. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to Sidebar](#sidebar) [Skip to Content](#content) [![PPC Land](https://ppc.land/content/images/2026/04/PPC-Land-logo-2.png)](https://ppc.land) ![Guardrails screen AI inputs, outputs and actions, but detectors were evaded up to 100% in one study](/content/images/size/w2000/2026/11/c-land-guardrails-explainer-cocktail-strainer-slipped-ice-cube-caught-olive.jpg) Guardrails screen AI inputs, outputs and actions, but detectors were evaded up to 100% in one study # Guardrails Guardrails are controls placed around an AI model or agent that check inputs, outputs and actions against set rules, and block what falls outside that policy. * [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/) by [Luis Rijo](https://ppc.land/author/luis/) [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/) [Luis Rijo](/author/luis/) Luís Rijo has written PPC Land daily since founding it in 2016. Over 10,000 articles, funded by readers, no sponsored coverage. Tips and corrections: luis@ppc.land + [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/danielrijo) * • * 9 min read * [Share on X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&text=Guardrails) * [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&quote=Guardrails) * [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&summary=Guardrails) * [Share on Pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&description=Guardrails) * [Email](mailto:?subject=Guardrails&body=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F) **Guardrails** are the controls that sit around an artificial intelligence (AI) system and decide what it is allowed to receive, say and do. In practice they are software layers, separate from the model itself, that inspect a user's prompt before it reaches a [large language model](https://ppc.land/llm/) (LLM), inspect the answer before it reaches the user, and, for AI agents, inspect each action before it executes. They exist because training cannot fully fix a language model's behaviour: the model that drafts a product description can be talked into inventing a refund policy or leaking personal data. Guardrails enforce limits from outside. The road-safety metaphor is used loosely. In advertising it also covers brand controls on AI-written ads and budget caps on buying agents. ## How guardrails work Most guardrail systems check content at up to five points, a structure NVIDIA's open-source NeMo Guardrails toolkit makes explicit in its documentation. * **Input rails** screen the user's message. They look for prompt attacks such as jailbreaks, banned topics and personal data that should not be sent to the model. * **Dialog rails** steer the conversation itself, for example forcing a scripted answer on a medical question. * **Retrieval rails** filter documents pulled from a knowledge base in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) before the model reads them, a defence against [prompt injection](https://ppc.land/prompt-injection/) hidden in third-party content. * **Execution rails** check what an agent sends to a tool, such as an API call, and what comes back. * **Output rails** screen the model's reply before display, blocking or rewriting harmful, off-topic or ungrounded text. The checks themselves come in three broad kinds. Deterministic rules are the oldest: keyword lists, regular expressions for card numbers or email addresses, allowlists of permitted domains. Classifier models are now the core of most products. Meta's Llama Guard, described in a paper submitted on December 7, 2023, is a Llama 2 model with 7 billion parameters fine-tuned to label both prompts and responses against a safety risk taxonomy that operators can adjust. A third kind uses one LLM to judge another, which is flexible but slow and itself open to manipulation. Commercial services package these into configurable...

Tips and corrections: luis@ppc.land + [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/danielrijo) * • * 9 min read * [Share on X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&text=Guardrails) * [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&quote=Guardrails) * [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&summary=Guardrails) * [Share on Pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F&description=Guardrails) * [Email](mailto:?subject=Guardrails&body=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fguardrails%2F) **Guardrails** are the controls that sit around an artificial intelligence (AI) system and decide what it is allowed to receive, say and do. In practice they are software layers, separate from the model itself, that inspect a user's prompt before it reaches a [large language model](https://ppc.land/llm/) (LLM), inspect the answer before it reaches the user, and, for AI agents, inspect each action before it executes. They exist because training cannot fully fix a language model's behaviour: the model that drafts a product description can be talked into inventing a refund policy or leaking personal data. Guardrails enforce limits from outside. The road-safety metaphor is used loosely. In advertising it also covers brand controls on AI-written ads and budget caps on buying agents. ## How guardrails work Most guardrail systems check content at up to five points, a structure NVIDIA's open-source NeMo Guardrails toolkit makes explicit in its documentation. * **Input rails** screen the user's message. They look for prompt attacks such as jailbreaks, banned topics and personal data that should not be sent to the model. * **Dialog rails** steer the conversation itself, for example forcing a scripted answer on a medical question. * **Retrieval rails** filter documents pulled from a knowledge base in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) before the model reads them, a defence against [prompt injection](https://ppc.land/prompt-injection/) hidden in third-party content. * **Execution rails** check what an agent sends to a tool, such as an API call, and what comes back. * **Output rails** screen the model's reply before display, blocking or rewriting harmful, off-topic or ungrounded text. The checks themselves come in three broad kinds. Deterministic rules are the oldest: keyword lists, regular expressions for card numbers or email addresses, allowlists of permitted domains. Classifier models are now the core of most products. Meta's Llama Guard, described in a paper submitted on December 7, 2023, is a Llama 2 model with 7 billion parameters fine-tuned to label both prompts and responses against a safety risk taxonomy that operators can adjust. Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open WebUI vs LibreChat vs AnythingLLM: 3 Picks [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 5, 2026 · 27 min read [Open WebUI shipped v0.13.0](https://openwebui.com/), and the project’s own release post says the update puts “a desktop, a browser, and Git beside the chat” for a team’s models. That one phrase shows where the three leading self-hosted chat interfaces for open-weight models are heading. They no longer want to be a text box that talks to a model. They want to be the workspace where models do things. LibreChat sits on a v0.8.9 release candidate (rc1 landed October 26), with v0.8.8 reported as the latest stable build on October 1. AnythingLLM reached v1.19.0 on October 26 and now ships a built-in local inference path in its Docker image. All three are free to self-host, all three talk to the same open-weight models, and all three change weekly. Picking the wrong one costs you a migration, so the details below matter. If you already run a local model server and want a browser front end, our walkthrough of [llama.cpp and Open WebUI](https://shattered.io/llama-cpp-server-open-webui-gguf-12-steps-2026/) shows the plumbing. The next question is whether Open WebUI should be the interface you standardize on, or whether LibreChat or AnythingLLM fits your team better. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Open WebUI vs LibreChat vs AnythingLLM: The Short Answer Pick Open WebUI if you run a team server and want the fastest-moving feature set. Its release cadence is the quickest of the three, with v0.12.0 on October 10 and v0.13.0 on November 3. Pick LibreChat if you route traffic across several model providers and care about agent tooling controls, because its latest release candidate adds MCP Apps, stricter tool-approval controls, and opt-in redaction of personal data in agent messages. Pick AnythingLLM if you want one person’s laptop or a small office box to work with the least setup, since the desktop app now bundles its own local engine and the Docker build gained a built-in Lemonade path in v1.19.0. That summary hides real trade-offs. Open WebUI’s licensing deserves a careful read, LibreChat’s newest build is still a release candidate, and AnythingLLM’s hosted cloud tiers cost money even though the software does not. No project publishes a standard benchmark for its interface layer, and the sources we checked contain no independent lab test of these three. Vendor-published numbers carry a label below. Claims that rest on a single report carry a hedge. ## Interface vs Runtime: What These Three Tools Actually Replace People searching for Ollama alternatives often mix up two layers. A runtime loads model weights and generates tokens. An interface gives humans (and teams) a place to chat, upload files, share prompts, and manage permissions. Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, and LM Studio’s server sit in the first layer. Open WebUI, LibreChat, and AnythingLLM sit in the second. Ollama makes the split easy to see. Its newest release in our research, v0.40.14, landed in early November (release listings disagree on whether that was November 2 or 3). The changes center on Claude Code launching, cloud web-search handling, and sampler defaults. None of that is a chat interface feature. Ollama’s own site says it serves 8.9 million developers and has raised $88 million, which shows how big the runtime layer has become. Our [Ollama vs LM Studio vs llama.cpp vs vLLM runtime comparison](https://shattered.io/ollama-vs-lm-studio-vs-llama-cpp-vs-vllm-local-llm-runtimes-2026/) covers that layer in depth, so this piece stays on the front end. Infra & Chips.content: # Supermicro's New Inference Racks to Use SambaNova SN50 Chips Supermicro has entered a strategic collaboration with AI chip company SambaNova to build and sell disaggregated AI inference systems. The partnership will see Supermicro integrate SambaNova’s fifth-generation SN50 Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit (RDU) chips alongside NVIDIA GPUs. The collaboration includes a planned order of 10,000 RDU chips from SambaNova. The resulting inference racks will be part of Supermicro’s Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS), a framework for creating optimised server and storage systems. The new systems are designed to improve AI inference performance within existing data centre power and cooling envelopes. RDUs are purpose-built for high-performance inference and can serve large models at high speed without requiring extreme rack power density. ### A heterogeneous approach to AI The collaboration creates a heterogeneous computing architecture where different processors are optimised for specific tasks. Supermicro’s systems will use NVIDIA GPUs to read the initial AI prompt in the prefill phase and then use SambaNova SN50 chips to write the response quickly during the decode phase. This division of labour is intended to drastically improve overall system performance and efficiency for inference workloads. “Supermicro is committed to delivering flexible, high-performance AI infrastructure that supports the evolving requirements of our customers,” says Charles Liang, President and CEO of Supermicro. “Our collaboration with SambaNova expands our broad DCBBS portfolio by enabling heterogeneous architectures that integrate GPU computing with specialised inference acceleration, helping customers deploy efficient, scalable AI solutions.” Operators can add inference capacity without waiting for next-generation data centre builds that may be constrained by power and cooling availability. > Agentic AI is the next wave of inference, and it has to run everywhere. > > Rodrigo Liang, Co-founder and CEO, SambaNova ## Addressing data centre constraints A key aspect of the partnership is addressing the physical limitations of modern data centres. By using RDUs that do not demand extreme power density, Supermicro aims to deliver solutions that can be deployed in existing facilities. This approach also allows data centre operators to extend the useful life of the GPUs they already own by augmenting their capabilities for inference. SambaNova and Supermicro state this strategy will allow them to deliver substantially more high-performance inference capacity by 2027 than would otherwise be possible. * The strategic collaboration is initially planning for 10,000 SambaNova SN50 RDU chips * The systems will pair NVIDIA GPUs for the prefill phase with SambaNova RDUs for the decode phase of AI workloads * Data Centre Compatibility: RDUs are designed to operate at high throughput without extreme rack power density, enabling deployment in existing data centres * Asset Longevity: The solution aims to extend the useful life of existing GPU deployments by offloading inference tasks * Support Model: Supermicro will integrate, test, deliver and support the systems, including providing on-site service ### Support and go-to-market strategy Supermicro will manage the full customer lifecycle, including the integration, testing, delivery and ongoing support for the systems. This includes providing on-site service for customers. SambaNova engineers will assist by getting models running and tuned on the SN50 chips and will help Supermicro with customer deployments. The companies will initially focus on NeoClouds and sovereign clouds as their primary markets. Infra & Chips.content: ## Since 1987: Covering the Fastest Computers in the World and the People Who Run Them ### TCI Media: Home of the Wire Publications ![Header Logo 1](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ai-600-300x73-1.webp) ![Header Logo 2](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/data-600-300x72-1.webp) ![Header Logo 3](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/qc-600-300x69-1.webp) ![Logo](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/hpc-logo-300x60-1.jpg) ## Off the Wire Press Releases ### November 5, 2026 ## Supermicro Launches KV Cache Solution with IBM and NVIDIA SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 5, 2026 — [Supermicro, Inc.](https://www.supermicro.com/) today announced a new KV cache storage solution with IBM and NVIDIA. The joint solution integrates Supermicro Petascale all-flash storage servers using AMD EPYC 9005 Series processors (Turin), IBM Storage Scale software, along with NVIDIA Dynamo inference framework software and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Supermicro-IBM-KV-Cache-300x157.jpg) KV Cache high-performance platform for large-scale AI inference Together, these technologies can dramatically reduce the time it takes AI models to begin generating a response, a critical advantage as enterprises adopt agentic and long-context AI workflows. Extending KV cache capacity beyond local GPU memory can improve GPU utilization and inference throughput, while enabling high availability of KV cache content and non-disruptive scaling of KV cache capacity. The result is a more scalable, resilient inference architecture that delivers faster, more responsive AI experiences. “As AI workloads expand from training to inference, enterprises and neoclouds deploying high-throughput inference workloads characteristic of agentic AI and long-context, multi-turn generative AI need to remove bottlenecks to improve GPU efficiency,” said Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro. “Our solution with IBM and NVIDIA clearly demonstrates these performance benefits.” Inference workloads consist of two phases: prefill and decode. During prefill, input text is converted into tokens and processed by the LLM to generate the intermediate key-value (KV) states needed for inference. By storing these previously computed KV states in a persistent KV cache, the system can reuse them instead of recomputing the same context for subsequent requests. Agentic workflows, coding assistants, long-context RAG, multimodal AI, and multi-turn applications can generate substantial KV state as they process large codebases, documents, conversations, images, and other context, quickly exceeding GPU and CPU memory and driving the need to offload KV cache to high-capacity, shared network storage. The KV cache solution from Supermicro, IBM, and NVIDIA provides this persistent storage layer, helping improve inference efficiency, throughput, and scalability while reducing redundant computation. Key customer benefits of the KV cache solution include: “Enterprises need a fundamentally better way to scale AI inference. Together, IBM, Supermicro, and NVIDIA are delivering a high-performance, resilient KV cache solution that helps customers maximize their GPU investments, scale independently of compute, and significantly improve infrastructure efficiency,” said Sam Werner, GM, IBM Storage. “This collaboration represents an important step toward making enterprise AI inference more scalable, reliable, and cost-effective.” “Agentic AI and long-context applications depend on reusing context efficiently across many steps, and NVIDIA Dynamo helps orchestrate distributed inference so enterprises can get more usable throughput from every GPU,” said Shruti Koparkar, NVIDIA AI Inference Product Lead. “By pairing NVIDIA Dynamo and Spectrum-X Ethernet with Supermicro Petascale storage servers and IBM Storage Scale, this KV cache solution creates a high-performance shared storage tier that can reduce redundant computation,...
